title: What Happens When You Type a URL

cards.title: One press of Enter
cards.body:
You type `https://www.example.com/news` and press **Enter**. Less than a second later, the page is on your screen.

In that second, almost everything in this course happens: binary, addresses, NAT, packets, routers, DNS, ports, TCP, TLS and HTTP. In this lesson you'll follow the whole journey, step by step, and do each part yourself.

cards.title: Reading the address
cards.body:
The web address you type is called a **URL** (Uniform Resource Locator). `https://www.example.com/news` has three parts:

- `https` is the **scheme**: which protocol to use. HTTPS means HTTP inside TLS, on port 443 unless the URL says otherwise.
- `www.example.com` is the **host**: the name DNS will turn into an IP address.
- `/news` is the **path**: which page to ask the server for.

cards.prompt: Match each part of `https://www.example.com/news` to what the browser does with it.

pairs.right: Ask for it in an HTTP GET request

cards.explanation: The **scheme** picks the protocol and port, the **host** is looked up with DNS to find the server, and the **path** goes into the HTTP request so the server knows which page you want.

cards.prompt: **Step 1: DNS.** The browser needs an IP address for `www.example.com`. Do the lookup yourself with `nslookup www.example.com`.
cards.intro: Simulated Linux terminal. Type help to see the commands you can use here.

commands.description: Ask DNS for the address of www.example.com
commands.output:
Server:		127.0.0.53
Address:	127.0.0.53#53

Non-authoritative answer:
www.example.com	canonical name = example.com.
Name:	example.com
Address: 198.51.100.10
Name:	example.com
Address: 2001:db8::10

success.question: Which IPv4 address will the browser connect to?

cards.explanation: `www.example.com` is a **CNAME** (an alias) for `example.com`, whose **A** record is `198.51.100.10`. It also has an IPv6 address, `2001:db8::10`, from its **AAAA** record, and many browsers would try that first. Either way, the lookup probably went through caches, a resolver and maybe the root, `.com` and authoritative servers, all in a few milliseconds.

cards.prompt: **Step 2: the first packet leaves.** Send the laptop's first packet (a TCP SYN to `198.51.100.10:443`) to the web server.
cards.explanation: Either ISP router works: routers pick the next hop from their routing tables. On the way out, the home router used **NAT** to swap the laptop's `192.168.1.20` and its temporary port for its own public address `203.0.113.7` and a public port, recording the swap in its NAT table. The router shows its public address here because that's the one the server will see.

cards.prompt: **Step 3: connecting securely.** Put the steps in order, from the first packet to the page arriving.

items.label: Laptop sends ACK: the TCP connection is open
TLS handshake: keys agreed and the certificate checked
Laptop sends an encrypted GET /news request
Server sends an encrypted 200 OK response

cards.explanation: First **TCP** opens a reliable connection with its three-way handshake. Then the **TLS** handshake agrees secret keys and proves the server is really example.com. Only then does the **HTTP** request travel, encrypted, followed by the response.

cards.prompt: **Steps 1 to 4 in one go.** Run `curl -v https://www.example.com/news` and watch DNS, TCP, TLS and HTTP happen. Then find which **port** curl connected to.
cards.intro: Simulated Linux terminal. Type help to see the commands you can use here.

success.question: Which port did curl connect to?

cards.explanation: `Connected to www.example.com (198.51.100.10) port 443`: port **443**, the standard HTTPS port. Reading from the top, you can see the whole course: the **DNS** answer (`198.51.100.10`), the **TCP** connection (`Connected`), the **TLS** handshake and certificate check, the encrypted **HTTP** request (`GET /news`), and the response (`HTTP/2 200`). (curl tried the IPv6 address first, but this network has no IPv6 connection, so it fell back to IPv4.)

cards.title: Rebuilding the page
cards.body:
The response comes back as a stream of **packets**, hop by hop, to your router's public address and port. The router's **NAT table** sends them on to your laptop.

Some packets may take a different route or arrive out of order. In Module 3 we said packets *usually* take one route, and now you know it doesn't matter either way: **TCP** uses its byte-counting sequence numbers to put everything back in order, and gets any lost data sent again. Then **TLS** decrypts it.

Finally the browser reads the HTML, sends more requests for the images and styles it mentions, and draws the page. Done: all in under a second.

cards.prompt: Put the whole journey in order, from pressing Enter to seeing the page.

items.label: TCP handshake with the server on port 443
TLS handshake: keys agreed and the certificate checked
The browser sends an encrypted GET request for /news
The server replies with 200 OK and the page's HTML
TCP puts the packets back in order and TLS decrypts them
The browser fetches images and styles, then draws the page

cards.explanation: Find the address (**DNS**), open a reliable connection (**TCP**), secure it (**TLS**), ask (**HTTP GET**), get the answer (**200 OK**), rebuild and decrypt it (**TCP and TLS**), then draw it. Every one of these messages travelled as **packets**, hop by hop, through your router's **NAT**, as **bits**.

cards.prompt: When a page won't load, the error tells you which step failed. Match each error to the step.

pairs.right: The server has no page at that path

cards.explanation: **Server not found** means DNS couldn't turn the name into an address. **Timed out** means the SYN never got a SYN-ACK back. **Not private** is a failed certificate check during the TLS handshake. And **404** means everything worked right up to HTTP, but there's nothing at that path. Each error points to a different step of the journey.

cards.prompt: Now the **reply**. The server sends the page to `203.0.113.7:40001`, the router's public address and port. **Router A is down.** Route the reply back to the laptop.
cards.explanation: With Router A down, the reply goes **B → C → home router**, which is a longer route than the request may have taken. That's fine: routes don't have to match in both directions. At the home router, **NAT** looks up port 40001 in its table, finds `192.168.1.20`, and passes the reply to the laptop, not the phone.

cards.title: Recap: How the Internet Works
cards.body:
You've followed a web page all the way from a key press to your screen:

- Everything is **bits**, grouped into bytes and written in binary or hex.
- Devices have **IP addresses**. Homes share one public address using **NAT** and ports.
- Data travels as **packets**, passed hop by hop by **routers**.
- **DNS** turns names into addresses.
- **Ports** pick the program. **TCP** makes delivery reliable, and **UDP** keeps it quick.
- **HTTP** asks and answers, and **TLS** makes it private.

Take the final quiz to finish the course. After that, you'll never look at a loading page the same way again.
